answers.question_text: What does the pattern of presence/absence found in T0.1.2a indicate for the characteristic's place in the human person and in the divine image?

slants.answer: Transgression's defining logic (Rom 4:15's 'no law, no transgression') indicates it is structurally RELATIONAL to a standard that exists independently of and prior to the person -- unlike guilt (a status one falls into) or sin (a failed aim), transgression's very possibility depends on an external boundary already set by God. This makes it, if anything, the MOST clearly derivative of the three families examined so far: it cannot even be defined without first defining God's law.

answers.question_text: What is the characteristic called in the programme, and what does the name signal about its essential nature?

slants.answer: Called 'Transgression' (G_transgression, M10). The name signals a spatial/legal metaphor -- STEPPING PAST or CROSSING a fixed line -- more literally boundary-oriented than either guilt (a status) or sin (missing a target); several occurrences show the literal spatial sense surfacing directly in translation ('bounds,' Jer 5:28; 'turned aside,' Acts 1:25).

answers.question_text: What do the primary Hebrew and Greek terms show at the definitional level?

slants.answer: parabaino/parabasis (Greek) roots literally in 'step beside/past' -- the family's noun form (parabasis) even states its own definitional dependency on law: 'where there is no law there is no transgression' (Rom 4:15).

avar (Hebrew, H5674D) is a general 'pass over/through/by' verb with the moral sense as one branch among many -- unlike chata (sin) or asham (guilt), which are dedicated moral roots, avar's moral use borrows a general motion-verb.

pasha (H6586/H6588) fuses 'transgress' and 'rebel/revolt' as a single lexeme -- the same root names religious sin and political insurrection, distinguished only by grammatical tense-environment, not by a different word.

answers.question_text: What directional, relational, or constitutional implication does the name carry?

slants.answer: 'Crossing/passing beyond' implies a FIXED, EXTERNALLY-SET line that exists prior to and independent of the person -- the person moves, the boundary does not. This is the sharpest directional implication of the three families read so far: guilt is entered, sin is missed, transgression is crossed.
pasha's 'rebel' sense implies REJECTED AUTHORITY -- not just crossing a line but repudiating the ruler who set it, whether a king (political revolt) or God (religious rebellion).

answers.question_text: What kind of inner-being phenomenon is the characteristic — an act, a disposition, a condition/status, a quality, or something else?

slants.answer: Predominantly a COUNTED STATUS/QUANTITY -- pesha (H6588, the family's largest and most frequent strong by far) is overwhelmingly a noun tallied in Amos's 'three... and four' formula, described as accumulating ('abundance,' 'multitude'), sealed in a bag, borne as a load. This is much closer to H_guilt's status-profile than to B_sin's agentive-power profile.

occurrences.verse_text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions.

answers.question_text: What inner posture does this movement require, as the evidence shows?

slants.answer: Acknowledgment of the specific transgression PLUS an explicit appeal to God's character (mercy) rather than to a completed legal procedure -- a more personal, less procedural posture than H_guilt's cultic-recognition formula.

occurrences.verse_text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions.

answers.question_text: What does the human-to-God direction of the characteristic show about the person's relationship with God?

slants.answer: The relationship is personal and appeal-based (mercy invoked directly) at least as much as procedural -- closer to B_sin's confession-and-grace pattern than to H_guilt's more ritual-bound one.

answers.question_text: In this verse, is the characteristic extended by one person toward another, and if so how does it operate in that extension? Record none if it is not.

slants.answer: Jacob's demand of Laban 'what is my transgression?' (Gen 31:36) treats transgression as a specific wrong one person could have committed against another -- the individual-against-individual register this family's own meaning block names.

occurrences.verse_text: Then Jacob became angry and berated Laban. Jacob said to Laban, “ What is my offense? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me?

slants.answer: At national scale, one people's revolt against another's rule (Moab, Edom, Israel against the house of David) is a collective, political form of the same person-to-person-scaled extension.

occurrences.verse_text: After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel.
So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.

answers.question_text: What inner conditions or orientations in the giver accompany genuine extension of the characteristic?

slants.answer: As with H_guilt and B_sin, no occurrence shows a virtuous inner condition accompanying an extension of transgression toward another -- every case (offense, revolt) is adversarial by definition.

answers.question_text: What does the evidence show a person must have received or become before they extend the characteristic?

slants.answer: For the revolt-cases specifically, the giver must first have decided to reject an established authority's rule -- a specific prior orientation (rejection of legitimate rule) this family names more explicitly than H_guilt or B_sin did for their own person-to-person cases.

occurrences.verse_text: So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time.

answers.question_text: In this verse, is the characteristic taken up by a person from another, and if so how does it operate in that uptake? Record none if it is not.

slants.answer: No occurrence clearly shows one person's transgression being 'taken up' from another the way H_guilt's Num 30:15 or B_sin's 2Tim 3:6 did -- this family's person-to-person cases (offense, revolt) are given/committed, not passed on or absorbed by another.

answers.question_text: What inner conditions accompany or block uptake of the characteristic from another person?

slants.answer: Not evidenced in this family -- consistent with T4.4.1's finding of no clear receiving-case at all.

answers.question_text: What is the inner-being state of the person who meets the characteristic from another but does not take it up?

slants.answer: Prov 18:19's Niphal 'a brother offended' is the closest case -- naming the person on the RECEIVING end of another's offense, though the verse describes the relational damage that follows, not an inner state of refusing uptake.

occurrences.verse_text: A brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city, and quarreling is like the bars of a castle.

answers.question_text: Does the evidence show the characteristic operating differently within existing relational bonds versus across relational distance or difference; if so, how?

slants.answer: Within a bond, it operates as covenant-breach with a named party (Israel's covenant, Judg 2:20; the everlasting covenant, Isa 24:5) -- a violation of an existing relationship's terms.

occurrences.verse_text: So the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he said, “ Because this people have transgressed my covenant that I commanded their fathers and have not obeyed my voice,
The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant.

slants.answer: Across political/national distance, it operates as outright REVOLT against an imposed rule with no prior personal bond assumed (Moab, Edom against Judah/Israel) -- a rejection of external authority rather than a breach of a covenant one had entered voluntarily.

occurrences.verse_text: And he went and sent word to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: “The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me to battle against Moab?” And he said, “I will go. I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses.”
So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time.

answers.question_text: Does the characteristic operate within covenantal contexts only, or does it cross covenantal boundaries, as the evidence shows?

slants.answer: Both: it operates within covenant (Israel's covenant with God) AND in purely political, non-covenantal contexts (one kingdom revolting against another's secular rule) -- this family shows the widest range of the three read so far, spanning theological covenant-breach to secular political insurrection under the very same lexeme.

occurrences.verse_text: So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.

answers.question_text: What does the evidence show about the relational scope of the characteristic — who is included and who is not?

slants.answer: Included: individuals (Jacob/Laban), nations against nations (the Amos formula's seven-plus-two peoples), Israel against God (the majority prophetic register), and even the cosmos as a limiting case that could in principle transgress but does not (the sea, Prov 8:29). Excluded: God himself (T0.1.2a).

answers.question_text: In this verse, does the characteristic operate in relation to other spiritual beings — angelic or adversarial — and if so how? Record none if it does not.

slants.answer: Yes, positively for angels: 'the message declared by angels' (Heb 2:2) stands behind the law whose transgression is then punished -- angels are the channel through which the very standard transgression violates was given.

occurrences.verse_text: For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,

slants.answer: No occurrence names an adversarial being as a transgressor or as inducing transgression.

answers.question_text: Does an adversarial-being code ever appear as an acting party in a verse carrying this characteristic?

slants.answer: No -- none found across this family's 118 occurrences.

answers.question_text: What does that pattern show about the characteristic being a site of adversarial activity?

slants.answer: Transgression, like guilt and unlike sin, shows no confirmed adversarial-activity pattern in this cluster's own textual evidence -- a genuine point of alignment with H_guilt against B_sin's positive finding.

answers.question_text: Does an angelic-being code ever appear as an acting party in a verse carrying this characteristic?

slants.answer: Yes -- angels are the acting party who declared the law (Heb 2:2), though in a mediating/instrumental role, not as transgressors themselves.

occurrences.verse_text: For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,

answers.question_text: What does that pattern show about the characteristic being communicated, strengthened, or mediated through angelic ministry?

slants.answer: This is the clearest positive angelic-mediation finding across the three families read so far: the STANDARD whose transgression carries penalty was itself given through angelic ministry -- angels are constitutive of the boundary's authority, a distinct and more foundational role than any 'strengthening' or 'communicating' of the characteristic to a person.

occurrences.verse_text: For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,

cross_family_or_cluster_flags.statement: This is the only confirmed positive angelic-involvement case (as opposed to adversarial) found across H_guilt (negative), B_sin (adversarial positive, angelic positive only via fallen angels), and G_transgression (angelic positive, in a mediating/authority-granting role distinct from B_sin's fallen-angel case) -- a genuinely distinct third pattern worth holding separately in any synthesis.

answers.question_text: In this verse, does the characteristic produce transformation in the person, and if so does it change the person's condition, their orientation to their condition, or both? Record none if no transformation is shown.

slants.answer: Produces a condition change via automatic retribution (Heb 2:2) -- the person's condition changes (penalty incurred) independent of any change in their orientation.

slants.answer: The recognition-group occurrences (Ps 51, Job 7:21) produce an orientation change -- turning to plead for removal -- without the verse itself narrating the underlying record's actual erasure.

answers.question_text: Is the transformation reversible or irreversible in the evidence?

slants.answer: Reversible via God's mercy -- 'blots out,' 'passes over' -- stated as a genuine erasure, not a mere covering-over.

occurrences.verse_text: I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you.

answers.question_text: Does this verse describe a sequence of inner states the characteristic moves the person through — a before, during, and after — and what are those states? Record none if no sequence is shown.

slants.answer: The same three-stage sequence already named at T1.2.2 -- committed-and-accruing (before/during) -> recognized/confessed (turning point) -> forgiven/blotted out (after) -- this family's clearest and most explicitly self-named sequence of any read so far.

occurrences.verse_text: For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me.

answers.question_text: In this verse, by what mechanism does the characteristic produce change — discipline, encounter, gradual formation, sudden transformation, or other? Record none if no mechanism is shown.

slants.answer: A declarative act of divine mercy (blotting out, passing over) is the mechanism -- sudden and unilateral, resembling B_sin's declarative-forgiveness mechanism more than H_guilt's ritual-procedural one.

occurrences.verse_text: Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of his inheritance? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love.

slants.answer: Automatic retribution (Heb 2:2) is a distinct, disciplinary mechanism with no described process at all -- consequence simply follows.

answers.question_text: Does the mechanism differ across contexts in the evidence; if so, how?

slants.answer: Yes -- mercy-based declarative removal and automatic retribution are the two poles, with the choice between them turning on whether the party is described as pleading/recognized or simply named as an offender under the law's operation.

answers.question_text: In this verse, does the characteristic operate in relation to suffering or affliction — as a response to it, a product of it, or a context for it? Record none if no such relation is shown.

slants.answer: Transgression is named as the direct CAUSE of national affliction -- 'the Lord has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions' (Lam 1:5).

occurrences.verse_text: Her foes have become the head; her enemies prosper, because the Lord has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions; her children have gone away, captives before the foe.

answers.question_text: What does the evidence show suffering doing to the characteristic in the person — and record no such effect if none is shown.

slants.answer: No occurrence shows suffering reducing or discharging transgression the way H_guilt's punishment-bearing did -- here suffering is transgression's CONSEQUENCE, not its resolution mechanism (resolution belongs to mercy/forgiveness instead, per T5.3.1).

answers.question_text: In this verse, does the characteristic participate in the longer arc of character formation and sanctification — shaping the person over time — and what does the evidence show of its role in that arc? Record none if no such participation is shown.

slants.answer: As with H_guilt and B_sin, only a negative-formation arc is shown -- transgression accumulates (T1.6.1) rather than forms virtue; no occurrence gives it a positive sanctifying role.

answers.question_text: In this verse, is the characteristic oriented toward an eschatological fullness — a future state toward which its present operation points — and what does its present experience anticipate of that fullness? Record none if no such orientation is shown.

slants.answer: Isa 59:20's turning-from-transgression at Zion's redemption is an explicit eschatological trajectory, and Isa 53:5's christological convergence-verse reinforces it.

occurrences.verse_text: “And a Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression,” declares the Lord.
But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.

slants.answer: Most occurrences show no eschatological orientation.
